summary: This informational memo documents a MAPOS version 1 extension, the Switch-Switch Protocol, which provides dynamic routing for unicast, broadcast and multicast traffic.

plainLanguage.summary: Switches chat with each other to work out the best paths for messages.

subtitle: Dynamic routing for unicast and broadcast/multicast in MAPOS networks

tldr.problem: In a multi-switch MAPOS environment, switches need to discover routes to all reachable destinations and forward both unicast and broadcast/multicast frames correctly without creating loops.
tldr.mechanism: SSP is a distance vector routing protocol for unicast frames (finding shortest paths) and uses a Virtual Reverse Path Broadcast (VRPB) spanning tree algorithm for broadcast and multicast frames.
tldr.outcome: Switches automatically learn topology, adapt to link failures with triggered updates, and ensure loop-free forwarding of all frame types.

today: RFC 2174 is an Informational document that extends MAPOS version 1 with switch-to-switch routing. It documents a complete routing solution for optical networks using SONET/SDH technology, combining distance vector unicast routing with spanning tree broadcast/multicast delivery. While MAPOS was not widely deployed in production networks, SSP demonstrates clean design principles for routing in networks with constrained header formats and simple topologies.

sections.title: Switch-Switch Protocol Overview
sections.content:
The Switch-Switch Protocol (SSP) is a dynamic routing protocol designed for multi-switch MAPOS environments. SSP is a distance vector routing protocol of the family that includes RIP, meaning each switch periodically exchanges its routing table with adjacent switches to discover routes.

SSP provides routing for two classes of frames: unicast frames (destined to a single node) and broadcast/multicast frames (destined to all nodes or a group). Unicast routing uses the distance vector algorithm to compute shortest paths. Broadcast and multicast routing uses a spanning tree algorithm called VRPB (Virtual Reverse Path Broadcast).

A key constraint in MAPOS version 1 is the absence of a source address field in HDLC frames and the lack of a TTL (Time To Live) field to prevent forwarding loops. VRPB overcomes these constraints by assuming all broadcast and multicast frames originate from a conceptual Virtual Source Switch (VSS), which is the switch with the smallest switch number in the network.
sections.plainLanguage: Each switch tells its neighbors what destinations it can reach and how far away they are. Switches pick the shortest path for regular messages. For broadcasts, all switches build a tree with the lowest-numbered switch as the root, and messages follow that tree to avoid loops.

sections.title: MAPOS Addressing for Multi-Switch Networks
sections.content:
In a multi-switch MAPOS environment, node addresses consist of two parts: a variable-length switch number and a variable-length port number. The overall address is 8 bits with the LSB always 1 (the HDLC address field terminator).

A unicast address is represented as 0 followed by switch number and port number, where the leading 0 bit indicates unicast. The switch number identifies which switch in the network, and the port number identifies the port on that switch to which the node is connected.

Broadcast addresses use all 1s (0xFF). Multicast addresses begin with 1 followed by the group address, where the leading 1 bit indicates multicast or broadcast.

For example, with 2-bit switch numbers, node N1 on port 0x3 of switch S2 (numbered 0x2) has address 01000011 binary (0x43). Node N3 on port 0x9 of switch S1 (numbered 0x1) has address 00100101 binary (0x25).
sections.plainLanguage: An address says which switch and which port on that switch. The first bit says whether it is a regular address (0), broadcast (1), or multicast (1). The remaining bits encode the switch and port numbers.

sections.title: Unicast Routing with Distance Vector
sections.content:
Unicast routing in SSP uses the distance vector algorithm. Each switch maintains a routing table with one entry for each reachable destination switch. Each entry contains:

  • The destination switch number
  • A subnet mask to extract the switch portion from the full address
  • The next-hop port (the local port connected to the adjacent switch leading to the destination)
  • The metric (hop count: 1 for adjacent switches, 16 or higher for unreachable)
  • Timers including EXPIRATION_TIMER and GC_TIMER (garbage collection)

Every FULL_UPDATE_TIME (10 seconds by default), each switch sends its entire routing table to all adjacent switches as a routing update message. When receiving an update from a neighbor, a switch adds 1 to each metric and compares the new metrics to its existing table. If a new metric is lower (shorter path), the entry is updated with the new metric and next hop. If the next hop is the same, the metric is updated regardless of value, resetting the expiration timer.

If no update is received from a neighbor for FULL_UPDATE_TIME × 3 (30 seconds), the route to that neighbor is marked unreachable (metric 16). The entry is kept in the table for another 30 seconds (GC_TIMER) before being deleted, allowing the switch to advertise the unreachable route to its neighbors.
sections.plainLanguage: Each switch keeps track of the fastest path to every destination. Every 10 seconds, it tells its neighbors about these paths. If a neighbor has a better path, the switch updates its table. If a neighbor stops answering for 30 seconds, the path is marked as broken.

sections.title: VRPB Spanning Tree for Broadcast/Multicast
sections.content:
Broadcast and multicast routing is based on the VRPB (Virtual Reverse Path Broadcast) algorithm, which constructs a single spanning tree rooted at the Virtual Source Switch (VSS), the switch with the lowest switch number in the network.

Each switch determines the VSS by searching its unicast routing table for the lowest switch number. It then identifies its place in the spanning tree: its upstream port (the port leading back toward the VSS) and its downstream ports (ports leading away from the VSS).

When a switch receives a broadcast or multicast frame, it forwards the frame to:

  • All its downstream ports (toward nodes and switches further from the VSS)
  • All its upstream ports (toward the VSS and ultimately other branches)
  • All locally attached nodes
  • But NOT the port on which it received the frame

This simple rule ensures loop-free delivery of broadcast and multicast traffic across the entire network.
sections.plainLanguage: Every switch finds the lowest-numbered switch (the VSS) and builds a tree pointing back to it. When a broadcast arrives, the switch sends it everywhere except back where it came from, so messages reach all nodes without looping.

sections.title: Preventing Routing Loops and Convergence
sections.content:
SSP employs several techniques to prevent slow convergence and transitive routing loops:

Split horizon with poisoned reverse: When advertising a route through the port from which it was learned, a switch advertises the metric as unreachable (16 plus the cost). This prevents a neighbor from believing that the learning switch has a path back through it.

Triggered updates: Instead of waiting for the next periodic update, a switch immediately sends an update when a local port fails, when a route becomes unreachable, or when a metric increases. This accelerates convergence when topology changes.

Forward delay timer: When a new VSS is discovered in the broadcast/multicast spanning tree, a switch suspends forwarding for a period (FORWARD_DELAY_TIMER, 30 seconds by default). This prevents transitive loops by waiting for all switches to synchronize their routing information.

Broadcast/multicast frame validation: Frames received on ports other than the upstream and downstream ports are discarded, providing defense-in-depth against loops.
sections.plainLanguage: When a switch tells a neighbor about a path, it warns that neighbor not to use it to reach the switch itself (poisoned reverse). If a path breaks, it tells neighbors immediately instead of waiting. It also pauses before using new tree roots to make sure everyone agrees.

sections.title: SSP Packet Format and Protocol Operation
sections.content:
An SSP packet is 4 to 512 octets, encapsulated in MAPOS HDLC frames with protocol type 0xFE05. The packet header (4 octets) contains a command field (1 octet: 1 for request, 2 for response) and a version field (1 octet, currently 1).

Following the header are 1 to 25 route entries, each 20 octets long. Each entry specifies a destination address, a subnet mask, and a metric (0 to 31, where 16 means unreachable and 17-31 are used for poisoned reverse).

A request packet asks for the entire SSP routing table. A response packet contains all or part of the sender's routing table. Responses are sent:

  • In response to a request (initial update when a port comes up)
  • Periodically every FULL_UPDATE_TIME (10 seconds)
  • As triggered updates when routes change or ports fail
  • On termination, with all routes marked unreachable

Upon receipt, a switch validates the version number and address family identifier (2 for unicast routes, 0 for full-table requests). It then processes each entry, checking for poisoned reverse information (metrics 17-31), creating or updating routing entries, and setting the broadcast/multicast spanning tree accordingly.
sections.plainLanguage: Switches send messages saying "tell me all your routes" or "here are my routes." Each route says a destination, how far away it is, and a mask. Metrics above 16 are warnings not to send traffic back through the sender.
